pages.description: Space Shuttle Atlantis completed STS-135, its 33rd and final mission landing on Runway 15 at Kennedy Space Center’s Shuttle Landing Facility on the morning of Thursday, July 21, 2011. pages.description: STS-73 marked second flight of U.S. Microgravity Laboratory (USML) and built on foundation of its predecessor, which flew on Columbia during Mission STS-50 in 1992. pages.text: Summary of the Major Laws of the Department of Labor | U.S. Department of Labor Skip to main content Summary of the Major Laws of the Department of Labor The U.S. Department of Labor (DOL) administers and enforces more than 180 federal laws. These mandates and the regulations that implement them cover many workplace activities for about 165 million workers and 11 million workplaces. Following is a brief description of many of DOL's principal statutes most commonly applicable to businesses, job seekers, workers, retirees, contractors and grantees. This brief summary is intended to acquaint you with the major labor laws and not to offer a detailed exposition. For authoritative information and references to fuller descriptions on these laws, you should consult the statutes and regulations themselves. Wages and Hours The Fair Labor Standards Act prescribes standards for wages and overtime pay, which affect most private and public employment. The act is administered by the Wage and Hour Division . It requires employers to pay covered employees who are not otherwise exempt at least the federal minimum wage and overtime pay of one-and-one-half-times the regular rate of pay. For nonagricultural operations, it restricts the hours that children under age 16 can work and forbids the employment of children under age 18 in certain jobs deemed too dangerous. For agricultural operations, it prohibits the employment of children under age 16 during school hours and in certain jobs deemed too dangerous. Search Twitter YouTube Facebook Instagram Flickr LinkedIn Swainson’s Hawks: a remarkable return to California’s Central Valley Oct 19, 2026 Swainson’s Hawks are medium-to-large raptors renowned for their elegant flight and extraordinary migratory journeys. Each year, these hawks travel thousands of miles between their breeding grounds in the western United States and Canada and their wintering sites in Central and South America. California’s Central Valley is especially critical to their life cycle, with 95 percent of the state’s Swainson’s Hawks nesting there. Upon arrival in the Central Valley, Swainson’s Hawks select nest sites near grasslands or agricultural fields, which offer abundant prey and shelter. During the breeding season, their diet consists mainly of rodents, rabbits, reptiles, and small birds, which are essential for raising their young. Outside the breeding season, they adapt by feeding primarily on insects such as grasshoppers, demonstrating remarkable versatility. Work Opportunity Tax Credit (WOTC) — This credit is available to employers for hiring individuals from certain target groups . Employers use Form 8850 to prescreen and to make a written request to the state workforce agency of the state in which their business is located (where the employee works) to certify an individual as a member of a targeted group for purposes of qualifying for the work opportunity credit. Disabled Access Credit — The Disabled Access Credit provides a non-refundable credit of up to $5,000 for small businesses that incur expenditures for the purpose of providing access to persons with disabilities. An eligible small business is one that earned $1 million or less or had no more than 30 full time employees in the previous year; they may take the credit each and every year they incur access expenditures. pages.text: The American flag and other national symbols | USAGov Skip to main content The American flag and other national symbols Get the facts about the U.S. flag and when to fly it at half staff. Learn about other national symbols. History of the American flag The flag of the United States is a symbol of freedom before which Americans recite the pledge of allegiance . The flag's 13 red and white stripes represent the 13 original colonies. Its 50 white stars on a blue background represent the 50 states. Each of the colors on the flag has a meaning: Red: valor and bravery White: purity and innocence Blue: vigilance, perseverance, and justice A star is added to the flag when a new state joins the United States. The flag was last modified on July 4, 1960, when Hawaii was incorporated as a state. Learn more about the evolution of the American flag and its earlier designs. How to raise the flag Follow these guidelines to properly display the American flag [PDF, 162KB]. When to fly the flag at half-staff The American flag flies at half-staff or at half-mast when the country or a state is in mourning. The president, a state governor, or the mayor of the District of Columbia can order flags to fly at half-staff.
